title: A baby's first weeks: check-ups, screening and when to seek help
intro: Newborn check-ups combine physical examination, feeding support and screening for conditions that may not be visible at birth. An appointment is also a chance to discuss your concerns and arrange follow-up. The timetable and services differ between countries, so confirm the local plan before leaving the birth facility. A normal earlier examination does not mean a baby cannot become unwell between visits.

sections.heading: Know which appointments are booked and who is responsible
paragraphs: Ask for a written plan naming the clinician or service, the appointment place and what to do if a visit is missed. In Germany, the early child examination programme includes a check immediately after birth, another between the third and tenth day, and a further check in the fourth to fifth week. These are German timings, not a universal schedule. After an early discharge or home birth, explicitly arrange the next assessment instead of assuming the hospital has booked it. Bring the baby's records and discharge information.

sections.heading: Understand the examination and its limits
paragraphs: The clinician reviews pregnancy and birth history, examines the baby and considers findings such as heart sounds, hips, eyes and, where relevant, testicles. Weight and general wellbeing are assessed alongside the family's observations. Some findings need a repeat examination or specialist referral even when a baby appears comfortable. Ask what was checked, whether anything remains uncertain and when referrals should happen. A screening result suggests the need for further assessment; it is not always a diagnosis, and screening does not detect every illness.

sections.heading: Discuss feeding, weight and everyday observations
paragraphs: Describe how often feeding is offered, whether the baby wakes to feed, swallowing, vomiting and changes in wet or dirty nappies. A midwife or clinician can observe a feed and review the weight pattern rather than judging one measurement alone. Some early weight loss can occur, but the amount, recovery and baby's condition determine whether help is needed. Ask for individual advice about breast or formula feeding and any recommended supplements. Do not dilute formula beyond its instructions or assume persistent poor feeding is simply a sleepy temperament.

sections.heading: Track screening results and the follow-up plan
paragraphs: Hearing screening, blood-spot tests and other newborn checks are offered according to local programmes and consent arrangements. Ask which tests were completed, which are still needed, how results arrive and whom to call if you hear nothing. An unclear hearing result may require repeat testing; it does not by itself establish deafness. Tell the team about family history and any concern about hearing or vision even after reassuring results. Keep appointments for abnormal or incomplete results, and ask for explanations or interpreting if the paperwork is difficult to understand.

sections.heading: Do not wait for a routine check when the baby is unwell
paragraphs: Difficulty breathing, blue or grey colour, being very difficult to wake, seizures or a rapidly worsening condition require emergency help. Fever or an unusually low temperature in a newborn, markedly reduced feeding, fewer wet nappies or increasing jaundice need urgent clinical assessment. Green vomit is an urgent warning sign. A newborn can have a serious infection without a fever. Explain the baby's age and what has changed when calling; follow urgent advice rather than waiting for the next booked check or trying home remedies first.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: arranging a check after early discharge
examples.text: A family goes home before the next scheduled examination. Before leaving, they ask who will perform it, confirm the date and take the discharge records. They also check how the blood-spot and hearing results will be communicated instead of assuming that no message means every result is normal.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: acting between appointments
examples.text: A newborn becomes harder to wake and feeds much less than usual. The carer seeks urgent medical help and describes the baby's age, feeding and wet nappies. They do not wait for tomorrow's routine visit simply because the previous examination was reassuring.

questions: Which examinations and screening tests are complete, and what appointments or results are still outstanding?
How is feeding and weight progressing, and what individual support does our baby need?
Which changes require urgent help, and which local service should we contact between visits?
